document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 9(1)-(9) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Risk management system
dataset_provision_summary: Providers must run a documented, continuous and iterative risk management process across the whole lifecycle of a high-risk AI system. It covers identifying and analysing known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating risks from post-market monitoring data, and adopting targeted mitigation measures so that residual risk is judged acceptable. Systems must be tested, including before being placed on the market, against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds (Art. 9(6)-(8)). Providers must consider likely adverse impacts on persons under 18 and other vulnerable groups (Art. 9(9)).

article_or_section: Article 10(1)-(4), (6) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Data and data governance; read with Article 4a(1)
dataset_provision_summary: High-risk AI systems trained on data must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that meet quality criteria. Data governance practices must cover design choices, data origin and collection, preparation steps such as labelling and cleaning, assumptions, the suitability of the data, examination for possible biases with measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them, and the identification of data gaps. Data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, as error-free and complete as possible, and suited to the setting in which the system is intended to be used.

document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 13(1)-(3) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Transparency and provision of information to deployers
dataset_provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be transparent enough for deployers to interpret their outputs and use them appropriately. They must come with instructions for use giving concise, complete, correct and clear information. At minimum this includes the provider's identity, the system's intended purpose, its capabilities and limitations, its accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risk circumstances, any capabilities for explaining outputs, human oversight measures, maintenance needs and log-handling mechanisms.

document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 14(1)-(4) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Human oversight
dataset_provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must be designed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them while in use, with the aim of preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights. Oversight measures must be proportionate to risk, autonomy and context, and may be built in by the provider or identified by the provider for the deployer to implement. The system must be provided to the deployer so that the people assigned to oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to understand its capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret its outputs, decide not to use or to override an output, and stop the system safely (Art. 14(4)).

document: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI)
article_or_section: Article 15(1), (3)-(5) (Chapter III, Section 2) – Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
dataset_provision_summary: High-risk AI systems must achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity and keep performing consistently throughout their lifecycle. They must be resilient to errors, faults and inconsistencies (possibly through redundancy or fail-safe plans), manage feedback loops in systems that keep learning, and resist attacks that exploit vulnerabilities. This includes, where appropriate, measures against data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples, confidentiality attacks and model flaws. Accuracy levels and metrics must be declared in the instructions for use.

document: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (DSIT White Paper, CP 815, March 2023; amended version)
article_or_section: Part 3, §3.2.3 A principles-based approach – Principle: Appropriate transparency and explainability
dataset_provision_summary: AI systems should be transparent and explainable to a degree proportionate to their risk. Transparency means communicating appropriate information about an AI system (how, when and for what it is used); explainability means relevant parties can access, interpret and understand its decision-making. Regulators should have enough information to give effect to the other principles. Affected parties should be able to get enough information to enforce their rights. Regulators may ask life cycle actors to provide information in a required form, including through product labelling.
